# Synopsis

Nell Hartley has six weeks, a per-diem, and Notebook 12, and the arithmetic is unforgiving: thirty-one working days to produce the one thing the Regional Survey's grant now depends on — a single signed sheet, no margin annotations, before the funding review closes the file for good. Form 9 has boxes for surveyor, resident, acreage. It has no box for the fact that the valley will not hold still, and that any reading taken in daylight is honest only until dark. She spends her first day at Stone Three doing the work properly — nineteen readings, each named to its stone, three checked again at dusk and found, briefly, to agree. Rosa Vane, who holds the countersignature the Survey needs and has withheld it for nine years, offers tea twice, asks after Nell's coat, and says no without explaining why. By dawn the valley has already answered for her: two of yesterday's readings no longer match, the old figures struck through and kept legible, since the notebook permits correction and forbids erasure. A wall-mender who knows all nine stones by number corrects Nell's chainage without looking up, and mentions a notebook from the last survey that was never filed. Over a second cup of tea, Rosa Vane explains her refusal in figures rather than fear — levies, acreage, nine years of arithmetic. For readers who like their strangeness filed in triplicate: this is a book for anyone who has loved *Piranesi*, *Winter's Bone*, or *The Employees*.


# Chapter 1 — Stone Three, Full Day

Four hours east of the district office the road stops pretending, and Nell Hartley got down with her case and opened Notebook 12 to the first page. She wrote the date. She wrote *fine, light southwest wind, cloud after noon*. Then she wrote *unopened*, because it had been until that moment, and a notebook that does not say when it began is an argument waiting to happen.

Arthur Penn’s covering letter ran to five numbered points. The fourth required one sheet, signed, no annotations in the margin. The fifth restated the review date, which she copied into the notebook under the weather, where it looked smaller than it was.

Form 9 she read twice. It had a box for the surveyor, a box for the resident, a box for acreage, and nowhere at all to say *this figure was true at the hour it was taken*. In the notebook’s margin — not on the form, the form allowed nothing — she wrote: *will need a box for uncertainty. None provided.*

The brief’s summary page gave her the figure she had half expected and underlined anyway: *no resident countersignature, nine years*.

She walked out at first light and found Stone Three where the eighth sheet said it would be, which she noted as a courtesy to the eighth sheet. She occupied it for a full day.

Nineteen readings. Stone Three, 412. Stone Three, 406. The stone named before the figure every time, because a reading that does not name its stone is not a measurement, and she had been doing this long enough to know which rules were pedantry and which were the whole job.

At dusk, with light still on the instrument, she went back through and took three of the nineteen again. Three identical figures. She wrote *holds exactly* beside them and felt, briefly, like someone who was being told something politely.

Rosa Vane met her on the track with a lamp she did not appear to need.

“You’ll have tea,” Rosa said. “Is it still raining in the district? They always say it is.”

“It wasn’t when I left.”

“It will be by the time you go back.” Rosa said nothing about the instrument, the case, or the nineteen readings, and asked instead whether the road had been bad at the bridge.

At the door she offered tea a second time. Hartley declined a second time and explained Form 9: the countersignature page, one signature, no acreage stated without it, no sheet filed at all.

“No,” said Rosa Vane, pleasantly, and did not say why. “Have you a dry coat?”

Walking back in the dark, Hartley did the arithmetic, which was the part of the day she trusted. Six weeks was thirty-one working days. She had spent one of them acquiring nineteen figures that held exactly, that named their stone, and that she could not file.


# Chapter 2 — Struck Through, Kept Legible

At first light Hartley set up on Stone Three and re-ran the three bearings that had held exactly at dusk: the ridge notch, the fold at the beck, the corner of the lower wall. She took each twice, as instructed by nobody but herself.

Two disagreed. The ridge notch came back 417 against yesterday’s 412; the wall corner 398 against 406. She drew a single rule through each old figure, left it perfectly readable, and wrote the new one beneath. The beck held. She did not record relief, there being no box for it.

Counting up the page, she made it nine strikethroughs in two days. At the top of the sheet she wrote, in capitals, *Notebook 12 is filed with the map* — a note addressed to herself at some future hour when a clean page would look like a kindness.

She walked to Stone Seven and took the ridge notch again from there: 344. She entered all three with their stones named, Stone Three twice and Stone Seven once, because a figure without a stone is a rumour.

Below the beck a man was setting coping on a wall under repair. “Chainage two-eighty from the gate,” she said, aloud, the way one says a number to keep it.

“Two-ninety-one.” He did not look up. Then he did. “Sorry. Habit.”

His name was Sam Ord. She named stones at him — four, six, nine — and he gave their positions without pause, then the other six unasked. She asked who took the eleventh sheet. “Rained the whole of that week,” he said. “Cleared by the Thursday. You could see the top of the ridge for about an hour.”

“Where’s the notebook for it?”

“In the valley. In a drawer. Numbered eleven.” He weighed a stone in both hands. “These copings want laying flat side down. Everyone lays them wrong.”

Rosa Vane came down with tea on a tray and poured without asking. Hartley asked about Form 9 a second time.

“Filed acreage, upper holdings, four hundred and six acres,” Rosa said. “Drainage levy, one pound eleven the acre, assessed yearly. Nine years.”

“That’s—”

“Three thousand six hundred and some. On ground we’ve had the use of rather less of since the night that sheet went out.” She refilled Hartley’s cup. Difficult relative; fond; nothing for the district office.

Hartley opened Notebook 12 and wrote the levy figures on the facing page, opposite her own ruled-through columns, and looked at the two sets of numbers sitting there together. The refusal to sign was not superstition. It was an invoice, nine years outstanding, and no one had ever sent it anywhere.


# Chapter 3 — What the Stones Fix

Four days before the deadline Hartley laid every reading in Notebook 12 out across the table in two groups: those named to a stone, and those tied to a landmark. Between them she ruled a single line. Below the line went bearings taken from the gate, the beck, the shoulder of the barn. Above the line, forty-one figures, each with a stone in front of it.

She drew the sheet from what was left. Stone One through Stone Nine, sited and numbered; the ridge, because the ridge is agreed; every reading attributed to the stone it came from. The acreage box she inked a border around and left empty, which took longer than filling it would have.

Sam Ord came to the door at eleven with a notebook under his coat and did not take tea. He said he had kept the corrections out of his submission — the dawn figures that disagreed with the dusk figures, nine years of them, the ones that would have shown the ground moving — so the eleventh sheet went to the registry clean.

“I stayed,” he said, “because the signature I talked Rosa Vane into is still being paid off in levies by people who feed me.” He put Notebook 11 on the table. He asked that it be filed nine years late.

Hartley wrote it down while there was light on the page: the admission, the date, his name. Then she turned back to the second week and drew one rule through *a tenant, name unknown*, leaving it legible, and wrote *Sam Ord, contracted cartographer, eleventh sheet* beside it.

Rosa Vane read the sheet at the kitchen table for a long time, tracing the empty box with one finger. “There’s no acreage here,” she said. “Nothing on this a man could assess.” Hartley offered the pen. Rosa Vane countersigned Form 9 and pushed it back without comment.

The covering note to Arthur Penn ran to numbered points, all of them negative. One: this sheet claims no acreage. Two: it claims no boundary not fixed by a benchmark stone. Three: Notebook 12 accompanies it with all corrections struck through and legible. Four: Notebook 11, submitted late by its author, is enclosed.

With the sheet still flat on her table she walked up to Stone Three in the last of the daylight and shot the ridge notch: 417. The same figure she had drawn that morning. The valley was holding, as it always held, until dark.

She carried sheet, Form 9, Notebook 12 and Notebook 11 down to the track end and gave the bundle to the carrier with both hands. She stood there until the bundle crossed the ridge, still lit.

After dark the ground let go of everything the sheet had declined to name. She heard nothing. There was nothing to hear. Inside the valley, with no instrument worth lifting until morning, she opened the spare pages and wrote: *19:40. Clear, no wind.* Then nothing else.
